content: Diabetes is a chronic health condition in which blood glucose (blood sugar) levels become too high because the body does not make enough insulin or does not use insulin effectively. The main types are type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, and gestational diabetes.

Common symptoms of diabetes can include increased thirst, increased hunger, frequent urination, fatigue, blurred vision, unexplained weight loss, numbness or tingling in the hands or feet, and sores that do not heal. Some people, especially those with type 2 diabetes, may have few or no noticeable symptoms.

Diabetes has different causes and risk factors depending on the type. Type 1 diabetes is associated with an autoimmune reaction that damages insulin-producing cells. Risk factors for type 2 diabetes can include family history, overweight or obesity, physical inactivity, high blood pressure, and certain other health conditions. Gestational diabetes can occur during pregnancy.

Type 1 diabetes currently cannot be prevented. For people with prediabetes or increased risk of type 2 diabetes, healthy eating, regular physical activity, and achieving or maintaining a healthy weight when appropriate can help prevent or delay type 2 diabetes.

Diabetes is diagnosed using blood glucose tests. Common tests include the A1C test, fasting plasma glucose test, and in some situations an oral glucose tolerance test or random plasma glucose test. A healthcare professional should interpret test results and confirm a diagnosis.

Diabetes management focuses on keeping blood glucose within an appropriate target range and reducing the risk of complications. Depending on the type and individual situation, management may include healthy eating, physical activity, blood glucose monitoring, prescribed medicines or insulin, regular medical checkups, and diabetes self-management education and support.

A person with possible symptoms of diabetes or risk factors should discuss testing with a healthcare professional. People already diagnosed with diabetes should follow their healthcare team's management plan. Severe symptoms, very high or very low blood sugar, or signs of diabetic ketoacidosis such as high ketones require urgent medical attention.

Hypertension, also called high blood pressure, is a condition in which the pressure in the blood vessels remains too high. It is common and can increase the risk of heart disease, stroke, kidney disease, and other health problems.

Most people with hypertension do not have noticeable symptoms. Very high blood pressure can sometimes be associated with severe headache, blurred vision, chest pain, dizziness, difficulty breathing, nausea, vomiting, confusion, or other symptoms.

Risk factors for hypertension can include older age, family history, overweight or obesity, physical inactivity, a diet high in salt, tobacco use, excessive alcohol consumption, and certain health conditions such as diabetes or kidney disease.

Risk can be reduced by eating a healthy diet with less salt, being physically active, maintaining a healthy weight when appropriate, avoiding tobacco, limiting harmful alcohol use, managing stress, and regularly checking blood pressure.

Hypertension is diagnosed by measuring blood pressure. A healthcare professional may use repeated measurements on different days to assess whether blood pressure remains elevated and to evaluate associated health risks.

Management can include healthy lifestyle changes and, when prescribed by a healthcare professional, blood pressure medicines. Regular blood pressure monitoring and follow-up can help assess control and reduce the risk of complications.

People should discuss persistently high blood pressure readings with a healthcare professional. Very high blood pressure accompanied by symptoms such as severe headache, chest pain, difficulty breathing, confusion, or vision changes requires immediate medical attention.
Asthma is a condition in which the airways become inflamed and narrower, which can cause breathing difficulties. It is often a long-term condition, although symptoms can vary from person to person.
Common asthma symptoms include wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, and a feeling of tightness in the chest. Symptoms may come and go and can become worse during an asthma attack.

The exact cause of asthma is not fully understood. Risk factors and triggers can include allergies, family history, cigarette smoke, air pollution, cold air, exercise, respiratory infections, and exposure to certain substances at work.

Asthma cannot always be prevented, but avoiding known triggers and reducing exposure to cigarette smoke and other irritants may help reduce symptoms. Following an asthma management plan can also help control the condition.

Asthma is assessed using symptoms and medical history along with breathing tests. A healthcare professional may use tests such as spirometry or peak flow measurement to evaluate how well the lungs are working.

Asthma management commonly involves inhalers and avoiding known triggers. The appropriate treatment depends on the person's symptoms and severity and should be determined with a healthcare professional.

An asthma attack can become life-threatening. Urgent medical help is needed when severe breathing difficulty occurs or asthma symptoms are rapidly worsening and the person's usual reliever treatment is not providing adequate relief.

Migraine is a recurring type of headache that can cause moderate to severe throbbing or pulsing pain. It may occur on one side of the head and can be accompanied by nausea or sensitivity to light and sound.
Migraine symptoms can include throbbing headache, nausea, vomiting, sensitivity to light or sound, and sometimes an aura involving temporary visual or other neurological symptoms.

Migraine can have a genetic component. Possible triggers include stress, changes in sleep, hormonal changes, bright or flashing lights, loud noises, strong smells, skipped meals, caffeine changes, tobacco exposure, and some foods or medicines.

Identifying and avoiding personal migraine triggers may help reduce attacks. Maintaining regular sleep, eating regularly, managing stress, staying hydrated, and keeping a record of headache patterns can be useful for identifying triggers.

Migraine is usually evaluated using medical history, symptoms, and a physical and neurological examination. Additional tests such as CT or MRI may sometimes be used when a healthcare professional needs to rule out other causes.

Migraine management focuses on relieving symptoms and preventing additional attacks. Depending on the individual situation, treatment may include medicines and lifestyle measures recommended by a healthcare professional.

A new, unusually severe, sudden headache or a headache accompanied by neurological changes such as weakness, loss of alertness, or significant confusion requires prompt medical evaluation. A healthcare professional should assess recurring or changing headaches.
The common cold is a viral infection of the upper respiratory tract. Different respiratory viruses can cause colds, and symptoms commonly improve within about a week.
Common cold symptoms can include a runny or blocked nose, cough, sneezing, sore throat, headache, mild body aches, and usually a low-grade fever in older children and adults.
The common cold is caused by different respiratory viruses. These viruses can spread through respiratory droplets and contact with contaminated surfaces or secretions.

Risk of respiratory virus infections can be reduced by practicing good hand hygiene, avoiding close contact with people who are sick when possible, improving indoor air circulation, and taking appropriate steps to avoid spreading illness when sick.

Most common colds can be recognized from their symptoms and do not require a specific diagnostic test. Testing may be appropriate when symptoms could instead be caused by infections such as influenza or COVID-19, particularly for people at higher risk of severe illness.
Most common colds improve on their own. General supportive measures can include adequate rest and fluids and measures that relieve symptoms. Antibiotics do not treat viral colds.

Medical care should be considered for trouble breathing, dehydration, a fever lasting more than several days, symptoms lasting more than about 10 days without improvement, symptoms that improve and then worsen, or any severe or concerning symptoms.
Influenza, commonly called flu, is a contagious respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses that infect the nose, throat, and lungs.

Flu symptoms often begin suddenly and can include fever or feeling feverish, chills, cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, muscle or body aches, headache, and fatigue. Some people, especially children, may also experience vomiting or diarrhea. Not everyone with flu has a fever.

Influenza is caused by infection with influenza viruses and can spread from person to person, including through respiratory droplets. Anyone can get flu, but older adults, young children, pregnant people, and people with certain chronic health conditions have a higher risk of serious complications.

Annual flu vaccination is the main way to reduce the risk of seasonal influenza and its serious complications. Other measures include avoiding close contact with people who are sick, limiting contact with others when sick, and following appropriate respiratory hygiene and infection-prevention practices.

Healthcare professionals may diagnose influenza based on symptoms and clinical circumstances. Laboratory tests are also available to detect influenza viruses, particularly when testing may affect medical management or public-health decisions.

Most people with mild flu recover without needing medical care or antiviral medication. General management may include rest, staying home and avoiding close contact with others while sick, and following healthcare advice. Prescription antiviral medicines may be appropriate for some people, especially those at higher risk of serious complications or those who are very sick.

People with flu symptoms who are at higher risk for serious complications, are very sick, or are concerned about their illness should contact a healthcare professional. Emergency medical care is needed for warning signs such as difficulty breathing, shortness of breath, persistent chest or abdominal pain or pressure, confusion, seizures, severe weakness, or symptoms that improve and then become worse.
Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluid than it takes in and does not have enough fluid to function properly.

Common symptoms of dehydration include increased thirst, dry mouth, reduced urination, dark-colored urine, dry skin, tiredness, dizziness, and weakness. Severe dehydration can cause confusion, fainting, rapid heartbeat, or rapid breathing.

Dehydration can result from diarrhea, vomiting, excessive sweating, fever, increased urination, or not drinking enough fluids. Infants, young children, older adults, and people with certain chronic illnesses may have a higher risk.

Dehydration can often be prevented by getting enough fluids and increasing fluid intake during hot weather, exercise, or illness when appropriate. People who have difficulty keeping fluids down should seek medical advice.

Healthcare professionals may assess dehydration using symptoms, medical history, and a physical examination. Depending on the situation, blood tests may evaluate electrolytes and kidney function, while urine tests may help assess dehydration and its possible cause.

Treatment focuses on replacing lost fluids and electrolytes. Mild dehydration may improve with appropriate oral fluids, while severe dehydration may require medical treatment such as intravenous fluids.

Severe dehydration can be life-threatening. Immediate medical attention is needed for signs such as confusion, fainting, very little or no urination, rapid heartbeat, rapid breathing, or signs of shock.
Anemia is a condition in which the blood has a lower-than-normal amount of healthy red blood cells or hemoglobin, reducing the blood's ability to carry oxygen to the body's tissues.

Symptoms of anemia can include tiredness, weakness, pale skin, shortness of breath, headache, dizziness, fainting, chills, and sometimes an irregular heartbeat. Mild anemia may cause few or no symptoms.

Anemia can result from blood loss, reduced production of red blood cells, or increased destruction of red blood cells. Risk factors and causes can include iron or vitamin deficiencies, heavy menstrual bleeding, pregnancy, chronic diseases, inherited conditions, and certain medicines or treatments.

Some types of anemia can be prevented by maintaining adequate nutrition and addressing causes of blood loss or nutrient deficiency. Eating a varied diet containing sources of iron, vitamin B12, and folate may help prevent some nutritional anemias.

Anemia is commonly evaluated with a complete blood count and measurements such as hemoglobin, hematocrit, and red blood cell characteristics. Additional blood or other diagnostic tests may be used to identify the underlying cause.

Treatment depends on the type, cause, and severity of anemia. Depending on the cause, management may involve treating an underlying condition, correcting nutrient deficiencies, prescribed medicines, or other medical treatments recommended by a healthcare professional.

Persistent fatigue, weakness, shortness of breath, dizziness, fainting, unusual bleeding, or other symptoms that may suggest anemia should be evaluated by a healthcare professional. Severe breathing difficulty, chest symptoms, or fainting require prompt medical attention.

Obesity is a complex chronic disease involving excess body fat that can affect health. It is influenced by multiple factors, including health behaviors, genetics, medical conditions, medications, stress, sleep, and the environment.

Obesity itself may not cause specific symptoms, but excess body weight can be associated with health problems such as high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, sleep problems, and joint problems.

Factors associated with obesity include physical inactivity, unhealthy eating patterns, inadequate sleep, chronic stress, genetics, certain medical conditions, some medications, and environmental or social factors.

Healthy eating patterns, regular physical activity, adequate sleep, and stress management can support healthy weight. Prevention is influenced by many factors, so approaches may need to consider individual health and environmental circumstances.

Healthcare professionals assess obesity using measurements such as body mass index and other information about health and body composition. They may also evaluate related health conditions and risk factors.

Management may include healthy eating, physical activity, adequate sleep, stress management, behavioral strategies, and healthcare-supported treatment when appropriate. Treatment options depend on individual health needs and may include medical or surgical approaches.

People concerned about their weight or related health risks can discuss the issue with a healthcare professional. Medical evaluation is especially useful when excess weight is associated with symptoms or conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes, breathing problems, or joint problems.

High cholesterol is a condition in which there is too much cholesterol or an unhealthy balance of cholesterol and other blood fats in the blood. High levels of LDL cholesterol can contribute to fatty deposits in blood vessels and increase cardiovascular risk.
High cholesterol usually does not cause noticeable symptoms. A person generally needs a blood test to find out whether cholesterol levels are elevated.

Risk factors for high cholesterol include age, family history, certain health conditions such as diabetes and obesity, a diet high in saturated or trans fats, insufficient physical activity, and smoking.

Risk can be reduced through healthy eating patterns, regular physical activity, maintaining a healthy weight when appropriate, avoiding tobacco, and managing conditions that can affect cholesterol levels.
Cholesterol is evaluated with a blood test called a lipid profile or lipid panel. The test can measure total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides.

Management may include healthy lifestyle changes and, when prescribed by a healthcare professional, cholesterol-lowering medicines. Regular cholesterol testing and follow-up can help monitor management.

Because high cholesterol often has no symptoms, regular health checks and appropriate cholesterol testing are important. People with known high cholesterol should discuss their results and cardiovascular risk with a healthcare professional.

Gastroesophageal reflux occurs when stomach contents flow back into the esophagus. Gastroesophageal reflux disease, or GERD, is a more persistent condition that can cause troublesome symptoms or complications.
Common GERD symptoms include heartburn and regurgitation. Other possible symptoms include chest discomfort, nausea, difficulty or pain when swallowing, chronic cough, and hoarseness.

GERD can develop when the lower esophageal sphincter becomes weak or relaxes when it should not. Factors that may contribute include obesity, pregnancy, smoking or secondhand smoke, certain medicines, and hiatal hernia.

Some people may reduce reflux symptoms by maintaining a healthy weight when appropriate, avoiding smoking, identifying foods or habits that trigger symptoms, and following healthcare advice about eating and sleeping habits.

GERD is often evaluated using symptoms and medical history. If symptoms do not improve or complications are suspected, healthcare professionals may use tests such as upper gastrointestinal endoscopy or esophageal pH monitoring.

Management may include lifestyle changes and medicines recommended by a healthcare professional. Depending on the situation, treatment can involve changes to eating or sleeping habits, medicines that reduce or neutralize stomach acid, and in some cases surgery.

Medical evaluation is important for persistent or troublesome reflux symptoms. Prompt medical attention is especially important for chest pain, persistent vomiting, difficulty or pain when swallowing, vomiting blood, black or bloody stools, or unexplained weight loss.
Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining. It can be sudden and short-term or develop gradually over time, depending on the cause.
Gastritis may cause pain or discomfort in the upper abdomen, nausea, vomiting, feeling full quickly, loss of appetite, or indigestion. Some people may have no noticeable symptoms.

Common causes and risk factors include infection with Helicobacter pylori, long-term use of certain medicines such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, heavy alcohol use, and some autoimmune conditions.

Some forms of gastritis may be reduced by following healthcare advice about medicines that can irritate the stomach, avoiding excessive alcohol use, and addressing Helicobacter pylori infection when present.

Healthcare professionals may evaluate gastritis using symptoms, medical history, and physical examination. Depending on the suspected cause, testing may include tests for Helicobacter pylori, blood tests, stool tests, or upper gastrointestinal endoscopy.

Management depends on the underlying cause. Treatment may involve addressing Helicobacter pylori infection, changing medicines that contribute to stomach irritation under medical guidance, or using medicines recommended by a healthcare professional to reduce stomach acid.

Medical evaluation is important for persistent or worsening stomach symptoms. Vomiting blood, black or tarry stools, severe abdominal pain, fainting, or symptoms of significant blood loss require urgent medical attention.
Food poisoning is an illness caused by eating or drinking food or beverages contaminated with harmful bacteria, viruses, parasites, toxins, or chemicals.
Common symptoms include diarrhea, stomach cramps or abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever. Symptoms and their severity can vary depending on the cause.

Food poisoning can be caused by bacteria, viruses, parasites, toxins, or chemicals that contaminate food or drinks. Risk can be higher for young children, older adults, pregnant people, and people with weakened immune systems.
Food poisoning risk can be reduced by washing hands and surfaces, separating raw foods from ready-to-eat foods, cooking foods to appropriate temperatures, and refrigerating perishable foods promptly.

Many cases of food poisoning are evaluated based on symptoms and medical history. Depending on the illness and circumstances, healthcare professionals may use stool or blood tests to identify the cause.

Management often focuses on preventing dehydration by replacing lost fluids and electrolytes. Some illnesses may require specific medical treatment depending on their cause and severity, so healthcare guidance may be needed.

Medical care should be sought for severe symptoms such as bloody diarrhea, prolonged or frequent vomiting, signs of dehydration, high fever, or diarrhea lasting several days. Young children, older adults, pregnant people, and people with weakened immune systems may need medical attention sooner.

An allergy occurs when the immune system reacts to a substance that is usually harmless to most people. Common allergens include certain foods, pollen, dust mites, insect venom, medicines, and animal dander.

Allergy symptoms depend on the allergen and body system involved. They can include sneezing, runny or blocked nose, itchy or watery eyes, skin rashes or hives, swelling, coughing, wheezing, or digestive symptoms.
Allergies can be influenced by genetics and environmental exposure. A family history of allergies or related conditions such as asthma or eczema can increase the likelihood of developing allergies.

Avoiding known allergens can help reduce allergic reactions. Depending on the allergy, prevention may involve checking food ingredients, reducing exposure to environmental allergens, or following an individualized allergy-management plan.

Allergies are evaluated using symptoms and medical history. Depending on the suspected allergen, healthcare professionals may use skin tests, blood tests, or supervised challenge tests to identify the trigger.
Management depends on the type and severity of the allergy. It may include avoiding the trigger and using medicines or other treatments recommended by a healthcare professional.

A severe allergic reaction can be life-threatening. Emergency medical care is required for symptoms such as difficulty breathing, swelling of the throat or tongue, severe dizziness, fainting, or other signs of anaphylaxis.
Arthritis refers to conditions that cause inflammation or other problems affecting joints. There are many types of arthritis, including osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.

Common arthritis symptoms include joint pain, stiffness, swelling, reduced range of motion, and difficulty performing activities that involve affected joints. Symptoms vary depending on the type of arthritis.
Risk factors vary by type. They can include older age, previous joint injuries, obesity, genetics, certain infections, autoimmune processes, and other health conditions.

Not all types of arthritis can be prevented. Maintaining a healthy weight when appropriate, staying physically active, protecting joints from injury, and managing certain health conditions may reduce the risk of some forms of arthritis or related disability.

Arthritis is evaluated using symptoms, medical history, and physical examination. Depending on the suspected type, healthcare professionals may use blood tests, joint fluid tests, or imaging such as X-rays or other scans.

Management depends on the type of arthritis and individual health needs. It may include physical activity, physical therapy, weight management when appropriate, medicines, joint-protection strategies, or other treatments recommended by healthcare professionals.

Persistent joint pain, swelling, stiffness, or difficulty moving a joint should be evaluated by a healthcare professional. Sudden severe joint pain, major swelling, redness, fever, or inability to use a joint may require prompt medical evaluation.
Pneumonia is an infection of the lungs that can cause the air sacs to fill with fluid or pus. It can be caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, or other infectious organisms.

Common symptoms of pneumonia include cough, fever, chills, shortness of breath, chest pain that may worsen with breathing or coughing, fatigue, and sometimes nausea or confusion. Symptoms can vary by age and cause.
Pneumonia can be caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi. Risk of serious pneumonia is higher in young children, older adults, and people with certain chronic diseases or weakened immune systems.

Some types of pneumonia can be reduced through recommended vaccinations, hand hygiene, avoiding tobacco smoke, and managing chronic health conditions. Preventive measures depend on the cause and individual risk factors.

Healthcare professionals may evaluate pneumonia using symptoms, medical history, and physical examination. Tests may include chest imaging, blood tests, pulse oximetry, or testing of respiratory samples depending on the situation.

Treatment depends on the cause and severity. Bacterial pneumonia may require antibiotics prescribed by a healthcare professional, while other causes may require different approaches. Supportive care and monitoring may also be needed.

Medical evaluation is important for suspected pneumonia, especially when symptoms are significant or worsening. Emergency care is needed for severe difficulty breathing, blue or gray lips or skin, severe chest pain, confusion, or significant deterioration.

A urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection affecting part of the urinary system, such as the bladder, urethra, or kidneys. UTIs are commonly caused by bacteria entering and multiplying in the urinary tract.

Common UTI symptoms include pain or burning during urination, frequent or urgent need to urinate, lower abdominal discomfort, and cloudy or strong-smelling urine. Kidney infections may cause fever, chills, back or side pain, nausea, or vomiting.

UTIs usually occur when bacteria enter the urinary tract. Risk factors can include being female, previous UTIs, sexual activity, pregnancy, certain urinary tract problems, urinary catheters, and conditions that make it difficult to empty the bladder completely.

Some UTI risk may be reduced by drinking adequate fluids, urinating when needed, and practicing appropriate personal hygiene. People who have recurrent UTIs may receive individualized prevention advice from a healthcare professional.

Healthcare professionals may evaluate a suspected UTI using symptoms, medical history, and physical examination. Urine tests such as urinalysis and urine culture may be used to identify infection and determine the likely bacteria.

Treatment depends on the location and cause of the infection. Bacterial UTIs are commonly treated with antibiotics prescribed by a healthcare professional. Adequate fluids and other supportive measures may also be recommended depending on the person's condition.

Medical evaluation is important for suspected UTIs, especially when symptoms are persistent or worsening. Fever, chills, back or side pain, nausea, or vomiting may indicate a kidney infection and require prompt medical attention.
Vitamin D deficiency occurs when the body does not have enough vitamin D. Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium and supports healthy bones, muscles, nerves, and immune function.

Vitamin D deficiency may not cause obvious symptoms. When deficiency is significant or prolonged, it can contribute to weak or painful bones, muscle weakness, and in children problems with normal bone development.

Risk factors include limited exposure to sunlight, low dietary intake of vitamin D, darker skin, older age, certain digestive conditions that affect absorption, and some medical conditions or medicines.

Adequate vitamin D can be obtained through appropriate food sources, fortified foods, and supplements when recommended. Safe sunlight exposure may also contribute to vitamin D production, but individual needs vary and excessive sun exposure increases skin cancer risk.

Vitamin D deficiency is usually evaluated with a blood test measuring 25-hydroxyvitamin D. Healthcare professionals may consider symptoms, medical history, diet, and risk factors when deciding whether testing is appropriate.

Management generally involves increasing vitamin D through diet, supplements, or other measures recommended by a healthcare professional. Treatment depends on the severity of deficiency and its underlying cause.

People with persistent bone pain, muscle weakness, or risk factors for vitamin D deficiency can discuss evaluation with a healthcare professional. Children with concerns about bone development should also receive appropriate medical evaluation.
COVID-19 is an infectious disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. It primarily affects the respiratory system but can affect other parts of the body as well.

Possible COVID-19 symptoms include fever or chills, cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, muscle or body aches, headache, sore throat, congestion or runny nose, nausea or vomiting, diarrhea, and changes in taste or smell. Symptoms vary among people.

COVID-19 spreads mainly through respiratory particles when an infected person breathes, talks, coughs, or sneezes. Risk of severe illness is higher for some older adults and people with certain underlying health conditions.

Risk of COVID-19 can be reduced through staying up to date with recommended vaccination, improving indoor air quality, practicing appropriate hygiene, and using additional precautions when illness or exposure risk is high.
COVID-19 can be diagnosed using viral tests such as antigen tests or nucleic acid amplification tests. Testing decisions may depend on symptoms, exposure, timing, and individual risk factors.

People with mild COVID-19 may recover at home with supportive care. People at higher risk for severe illness may benefit from early medical evaluation because specific antiviral treatments may be available when prescribed by a healthcare professional.

Emergency medical attention is needed for warning signs such as trouble breathing, persistent chest pain or pressure, new confusion, inability to wake or stay awake, or pale, gray, or blue-colored skin, lips, or nail beds.
Heart disease refers to several conditions that affect the heart. Common types include coronary artery disease, heart rhythm problems, and conditions affecting the heart muscle or valves.

Symptoms depend on the type of heart disease. Possible symptoms include chest discomfort or pain, shortness of breath, fatigue, dizziness, palpitations, swelling of the legs or feet, and reduced ability to exercise.

Risk factors vary by type but can include high blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, older age, and family history of cardiovascular disease.

Heart disease risk can be reduced by not smoking, being physically active, eating a heart-healthy diet, maintaining a healthy weight when appropriate, managing blood pressure and cholesterol, controlling diabetes, getting adequate sleep, and following healthcare advice.

Evaluation depends on the suspected heart condition. Healthcare professionals may use medical history, physical examination, blood tests, electrocardiography, echocardiography, stress testing, or other imaging and diagnostic procedures.

Management depends on the specific heart condition and may include lifestyle changes, medicines prescribed by healthcare professionals, procedures, or surgery when appropriate. Regular follow-up helps monitor cardiovascular health.
Sudden chest pressure or pain, severe shortness of breath, fainting, or other signs that could indicate a heart attack or another serious heart problem require emergency medical attention.

Thyroid disorders are conditions that affect the thyroid gland and its production or regulation of thyroid hormones. Common disorders include hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, thyroid nodules, and thyroid inflammation.

Symptoms depend on the thyroid disorder. Hypothyroidism may cause fatigue, weight gain, feeling cold, dry skin, and slowed heart rate, while hyperthyroidism may cause weight loss, rapid heartbeat, nervousness, sweating, and heat intolerance.

Causes vary by disorder and can include autoimmune conditions, thyroid inflammation, certain medicines, iodine imbalance, thyroid nodules, and other medical conditions. Family history can increase the risk of some thyroid disorders.

Many thyroid disorders cannot be completely prevented. Maintaining appropriate nutrition, avoiding unnecessary exposure to excessive iodine or certain substances, and managing related health conditions may support thyroid health.

Thyroid disorders are commonly evaluated with blood tests that measure thyroid-stimulating hormone and thyroid hormones. Depending on the condition, healthcare professionals may also use thyroid antibody tests, ultrasound, or other imaging or diagnostic tests.

Treatment depends on the specific thyroid disorder. Management may include medicines that replace or reduce thyroid hormone, treatment of underlying causes, monitoring, or procedures recommended by a healthcare professional.

Persistent symptoms such as unexplained changes in weight, unusual fatigue, rapid or slow heartbeat, temperature intolerance, or neck swelling should be discussed with a healthcare professional. Severe breathing difficulty, chest symptoms, or a very rapid heartbeat require urgent medical attention.

Depression is a common but serious mental health condition that can affect mood, thinking, daily activities, sleep, appetite, and interest in previously enjoyable activities. It can range from mild to severe.

Possible symptoms include persistent sadness or emptiness, loss of interest or pleasure, changes in appetite or sleep, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, irritability, and thoughts of death or suicide.

Depression can result from a combination of genetic, biological, environmental, and psychological factors. Risk may be influenced by family history, stressful or traumatic experiences, certain medical conditions, and other mental health conditions.

Depression cannot always be prevented. Maintaining supportive relationships, regular physical activity, healthy sleep habits, stress-management practices, and seeking professional help when symptoms persist may support mental well-being.

Healthcare professionals usually evaluate depression through a clinical assessment that considers symptoms, their duration, severity, daily functioning, medical history, and other possible causes. There is no single laboratory test that by itself diagnoses depression.

Treatment may include psychotherapy, medication, or a combination of both. The appropriate approach depends on the person's symptoms, preferences, and medical situation and should be determined with a qualified healthcare professional.

Persistent or worsening symptoms that interfere with daily life should be discussed with a healthcare professional. Thoughts of suicide or self-harm require immediate professional help or emergency assistance.

Anxiety is a normal emotional response to stress or perceived danger. Anxiety disorders involve excessive or persistent fear, worry, or anxiety that does not go away easily and can interfere with daily life.

Symptoms vary by anxiety disorder and may include excessive worry, nervousness, restlessness, irritability, difficulty concentrating, sleep problems, fatigue, muscle tension, sweating, trembling, dizziness, or shortness of breath.

Anxiety disorders can involve a combination of genetic, biological, environmental, and psychological factors. Stressful experiences, family history, other mental health conditions, and some physical health conditions may increase risk.

Anxiety disorders cannot always be prevented. Healthy sleep, regular physical activity, supportive relationships, stress-management strategies, and seeking professional help when anxiety becomes persistent or disruptive may support mental health.

A healthcare professional may evaluate anxiety by discussing symptoms, their duration, severity, triggers, and effects on daily life. A physical examination or additional evaluation may be used to check whether another health condition could be contributing to symptoms.

Treatment for anxiety disorders may include psychotherapy, medication, or both. Cognitive behavioral therapy is a commonly used evidence-based psychotherapy. Treatment should be selected with a qualified healthcare professional based on individual needs.

Persistent anxiety that interferes with work, school, relationships, sleep, or daily activities should be discussed with a healthcare professional. Immediate help is important if someone has thoughts of suicide or is in immediate danger.

Insomnia is a sleep disorder involving difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or getting adequate restorative sleep despite having an opportunity to sleep. It can affect daytime functioning and well-being.

Symptoms may include taking a long time to fall asleep, waking frequently during the night, waking too early, poor-quality sleep, daytime sleepiness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, anxiety, low mood, or irritability.

Insomnia can be associated with stress, changes in schedule or environment, shift work, travel across time zones, irregular sleep routines, insufficient physical activity, caffeine or nicotine use, electronic device use near bedtime, certain medicines, and other health conditions.

Healthy sleep habits may reduce the risk of insomnia. Helpful habits include maintaining a regular sleep and wake schedule, creating a comfortable sleep environment, limiting caffeine and nicotine near bedtime, staying physically active during the day, and managing stress.

Healthcare professionals may evaluate insomnia by discussing sleep patterns, symptoms, daily activities, medicines, and health conditions. A sleep diary can be useful. Additional testing may be considered when another sleep or health disorder is suspected.

Management may include healthy sleep habits and cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I). Depending on the situation, a healthcare professional may also consider other treatments or medicines. Long-term treatment should be guided by a healthcare professional.

People should discuss insomnia with a healthcare professional when poor sleep regularly affects daytime activities, concentration, mood, or overall functioning. Persistent sleep problems may require evaluation for an underlying condition.
Kidney stones are hard, pebble-like deposits that form in the kidneys when certain minerals and substances become concentrated in urine and form crystals. Stones can vary in size and type.

Symptoms may include sharp pain in the back, side, lower abdomen, or groin; blood in the urine; pain during urination; frequent urination; cloudy or bad-smelling urine; nausea; or vomiting. Some small stones may cause few or no symptoms.

Kidney stones can form when certain minerals are present in high concentrations in urine. Risk factors may include not drinking enough fluids, certain dietary patterns, previous kidney stones, family history, some medical conditions, and other factors that affect urine composition.

Drinking enough fluids can help keep urine diluted and may reduce the risk of many kidney stones. Depending on the type of stone, healthcare professionals may also recommend individualized dietary or lifestyle changes.

Healthcare professionals may use medical history, physical examination, urine tests, blood tests, and imaging studies to evaluate suspected kidney stones. Testing can also help identify factors that contributed to stone formation.

Management depends on the stone's size, location, type, and symptoms. Small stones may pass through the urinary tract without a procedure, while larger or obstructing stones may require medical treatment or a procedure to remove or break them.

Severe or persistent pain, blood in the urine, inability to urinate, fever, chills, nausea, or vomiting can require prompt medical evaluation. A blocked urinary tract combined with infection can be a serious condition.
